title: Install and your first project
description: Install the kikx CLI, create a project with kikx init, find components with kikx list and vendor their files with kikx add.
outcomes: Know what the install script does before you run it
Create kikx.toml with kikx init and read what it holds
Read kikx list to find a component and its fields
Vendor files with kikx add, its name and set options
See why kikx refuses to overwrite a file you own

checks.service: You ran kikx add {serviceComponent} for {name} with {portSet}
checks.role: You ran kikx add {roleComponent} named {roleName} with {timezoneSet}

recap: The install script downloads the kikx binary for your system. Read it, then run it in your own terminal.
kikx init writes kikx.toml: the project name, its default namespace and the folder files go to.
kikx list prints every component with its fields, defaults and examples.
kikx add renders a component with the real engine and writes plain files into your output folder.
kikx never overwrites a file you already have unless you add the force option.

steps.intro: Let's use kikx from a terminal. This page is a practice terminal: I type real kikx commands, the real kikx engine renders the files, and nothing touches your machine.
steps.terminal: Commands go here. I type each one letter by letter, then you see exactly what the CLI prints.
steps.files: Files the commands write show up on this side. Click one to read it.
steps.install: First, installing kikx. On macOS and Linux this one line does it.
steps.installNotice: The practice terminal doesn't run the installer: it would change your machine, not this page.
steps.installWhat: The script finds the latest kikx release for your system, downloads the binary and puts it on your PATH. Nothing else is installed, and you can read the script first.
steps.copy: Every command has a copy button. Use it to run the command for real in your own terminal.
steps.init: Every kikx project starts with kikx init. I give it a name; without one, kikx uses the folder name.
steps.initialized: kikx confirms the project and reminds you what comes next.
steps.toml: It wrote one file: kikx.toml, at the root of the project.
steps.tomlName: name is the project name you gave.
steps.tomlNamespace: default_namespace is used by Kubernetes components when you don't set one.
steps.tomlOutput: output_dir is the folder every vendored file goes into.
steps.outputDir: kikx created that folder right away, empty for now: {outputDir}.
steps.list: Which components can you add? kikx list prints them all.
steps.listItem: Each entry is category/component, the reference you pass to kikx add, with a short description.
steps.listFields: Under it, the fields you can set, each marked required or with its default and an example.
steps.listOthers: The same components power the app, so what you see here is what the builder offers.
steps.add: Let's vendor a Kubernetes Deployment. {flagName} names it, and {flagSet} fills in a field, here the image it runs.
steps.vendored: Vendored means the files are now in your project, rendered and ready to commit.
steps.deploymentFile: Here's the file, named after the component.
steps.imageLine: The image you set is in the file. Fields you left out took their defaults, like one replica.
steps.yours: These are plain files. Edit them in your editor and commit them; kikx doesn't keep a copy or sync anything later.
steps.addService: Your turn. Click the terminal and add a Service for the same app: kikx add {serviceComponent} {flagName} {name} {flagSet} {portSet}, then press Enter.
steps.serviceFile: A second file. The Service and the Deployment share the name {name}, so they find each other.
steps.rerun: What if I run the first command again?
steps.refused: kikx stops instead of overwriting the file you may have edited. Pass {flagForce} only when you want the fresh version.
steps.addRole: Your turn. Add an Ansible role with a setting: kikx add {roleComponent} {flagName} {roleName} {flagSet} {timezoneSet}.
steps.roleFiles: One component can write several files: the role has tasks, defaults, handlers and a template.
steps.timezoneLine: And the value you set landed in its tasks.
steps.done: That's the CLI loop: init once, list to explore, add what you need. Copy any command to try it for real.
